title: The Necessary Wardrobe
premise: Ansel Coldharbour, a celebrated restaurant critic who lost his sense of taste after his brother's unexplained death, has spent eleven years keeping an inventory notebook of everything he never said aloud. When a radio station plays an unfinished song only his dead brother ever wrote, Ansel realizes someone is alive who knows the music—and the truth about the night his brother drowned. Following the song through a fading coastal town, he must finally translate the one sentence in his inventory written in a language neither he nor his brother officially spoke, confess what he witnessed, and let the family house—sold and closing Friday—hold its last secret before it belongs to strangers.
about_author: U. M. Villalobos is the pen name of a former court stenographer from the Oregon coast who spent two decades transcribing other people's confessions before writing any of her own. 'The Necessary Wardrobe' is her second novel, following a well-received debut about a lighthouse keeper's widow.

chapters.title: The Inventory of Unsaid Things
chapters.summary: Ansel, POV, dines at a restaurant he cannot taste and writes a glowing review anyway, then returns home to add three new entries to his notebook of unsaid things. We learn his taste died the week his brother Theo drowned. Emotional beat: numb routine cracked by quiet grief.

chapters.title: A Song That Was Never Recorded
chapters.summary: Driving home, Ansel hears a radio station play a melody only Theo ever hummed, unfinished, never written down. He crashes into a ditch, unharmed, shaking. POV: Ansel. Emotional beat: vertigo—the past reaching into the present, proof that invisibility has failed him.

chapters.title: The House That Must Be Emptied
chapters.summary: Ansel's sister Marguerite arrives to stage the family house for Friday's sale, forcing him to confront Theo's locked room. She suspects he knows more about the drowning than he's admitted. POV alternates briefly to Marguerite. Emotional beat: sibling friction, guilt pressing against sealed doors.

chapters.title: The Man Who Hums
chapters.summary: Ansel traces the broadcast to a small AM station and finds the DJ, Ovid Reyes, who admits a man leaves anonymous tapes in his mailbox—recordings of songs no one has written yet, or so it seems. POV: Ansel. Emotional beat: cautious hope tangled with dread; first ally found.

chapters.title: What the Water Kept
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter, Theo's perspective in the weeks before his death: the brothers' private language, a woman named Lark, and Theo's fear of something he'd seen at the marina. Emotional beat: tenderness curdling toward foreboding as the reader learns what Ansel cannot remember admitting.

chapters.title: Lark Still Sings
chapters.summary: Ansel finds Lark Voss living under another name, teaching piano. She denies everything until he hums the song; then she plays it complete, with lyrics—in their childhood invented language. POV: Ansel. Emotional beat: recognition and betrayal; she was there that night too, and stayed silent longer than he did.

chapters.title: The Sentence in the Notebook
chapters.summary: Ansel rereads his inventory and finds the entry he wrote the morning after the drowning—one sentence in the invented language he can no longer parse. Marguerite discovers him burning pages and demands the truth. POV: Ansel. Emotional beat: rising panic; the confession he archived is now illegible even to himself.

chapters.title: Tapes for a Dead Man
chapters.summary: Ovid reveals the tape sender's return address: the marina office where Theo worked, still staffed by Harlan Pike, the owner who ruled the drowning an accident. Ansel confronts Harlan and remembers, mid-confrontation, what he saw. POV: Ansel. Climax begins. Emotional beat: fury breaking through eleven years of anesthesia.

chapters.title: Translation
chapters.summary: Climax. With Lark and Marguerite present in the emptying house, Ansel translates the sentence aloud: he watched Harlan's boat strike Theo's skiff and said nothing because Harlan held the note on their mother's debt. He reports it—to Lark, to Marguerite, and finally to a police officer who once ignored him. Emotional beat: devastating release; justice outside the law begins with speech itself.

chapters.title: Closing
chapters.summary: Resolution. The house sale closes; Harlan is investigated on old insurance fraud charges, not the drowning—imperfect justice. Ansel eats a meal and tastes it, faintly, for the first time in years. He gives the inventory notebook to Marguerite, blank pages forward. Emotional beat: quiet, earned grace; memory carried instead of buried.
